title: Project activities
body_markdown:
## Project activities

The August 2025 *Stormwater Model Update and Flood-Risk Area Identification and Prioritization* report identifies six concept-level flood-risk mitigation alternatives across three City-selected flood-risk areas. These alternatives were modeled and costed for planning purposes; the report states that additional design and evaluation will be required before a project is pursued.

[Information needed: Confirm the flood-risk mitigation concept that the City of Richfield is submitting for the Flood Hazard Mitigation Grant Assistance Program application.]

### Candidate concept-level activities and quantities

| Flood-risk area | Concept-level activity | Documented quantifiable output or configuration | Planning-level construction cost |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| Near Wilson Pond | **Concept A:** Lower the water level in Wilson Pond ahead of a storm event; modify the outlet by lowering the invert; and increase downstream storm sewer capacity. | A remotely accessible gate controlled using weather forecasts would provide approximately 5 acre-feet of additional storage ahead of a storm event, assuming a 24-hour drawdown period. | $8,853,000 |
| Near Wilson Pond | **Concept B:** Increase storm sewer capacity from Wilson Pond to Highway 494. | A single 5-foot by 5-foot box culvert is represented from Wilson Pond to Highway 494. | $11,536,000 |
| Near Wilson Pond | **Concept C:** Increase the number and capacity of storm sewer pipes from Wilson Pond to Highway 494. | Two parallel 5-foot by 5-foot box culverts are represented from Wilson Pond to Highway 494. | $17,333,000 |
| Northwest of Roosevelt Park | **Concept A:** Construct an underground storage chamber beneath the Roosevelt Park baseball fields and modify storm sewer connections to direct drainage to the chamber. | Approximately 354,000 cubic feet of underground storage, based on a 300-foot by 300-foot surface area, 5.25-foot depth, and 75% available stormwater-storage volume. | $15,491,000 |
| Near Woodlawn Terrace | **Concept A:** Construct an underground storage chamber beneath the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments and modify storm sewer connections. | Approximately 24,000 cubic feet of underground storage, based on approximately 8,000 square feet of surface area, a 3-foot depth, and 75% available stormwater-storage volume. | $1,540,000 |
| Near Woodlawn Terrace | **Concept B:** Increase storm sewer capacity from the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments to Wood Lake. | The concept increases pipe diameters from a current range of 3 to 4 feet to a range of 3 to 6 feet. | $7,440,000 |

### Activity considerations

The Wilson Pond concepts would require storm sewer changes from Wilson Pond to Highway 494 and would increase the volume and peak rate of discharge leaving the municipal boundary. The report states that further coordination with the City of Bloomington or MnDOT would be required because downstream routing to the Minnesota River has not been determined.

The Northwest of Roosevelt Park concept includes an outlet-control structure so that the underground storage can retain runoff and drain after a storm event. The Woodlawn Terrace underground-storage concept would require regrading of the parking lot and agreements with the owner of the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments.

The report characterizes all six alternatives as concept-level designs. It identifies further work that may include design optimization, utility-conflict evaluation, permitting review, and, in some cases, agreements with private landowners or other public entities.

title: Summary of flood damages
body_markdown:
## Summary of flood damages

### Flood-risk assessment basis

The August 2025 *Stormwater Model Update and Flood-Risk Area Identification and Prioritization* report evaluates potential inundation using an updated citywide PCSWMM model. The model simulates Atlas 14 2-, 10-, and 100-year 24-hour rainfall events, together with a Mid-21st-century 100-year moderate rainfall estimate (MCE100-year) 24-hour event. The respective precipitation depths are 2.83, 4.24, 7.50, and 10.20 inches.

Model peak water levels were used to delineate inundation areas in ponds, wetlands, and topographic depressions through level-pool mapping in ArcGIS. The report states that inundation mapping of sloped water surfaces along roadways and through the floodplain was not completed. Figures 3-1 through 3-4 of the report provide inundation maps for the four modeled events.

A total of 746 flood-risk areas were evaluated within the study area, of which 601 are within or primarily within the Richfield municipal boundary. The prioritization considered storm-system conditions, critical infrastructure, frequency of flooding, social vulnerability, and potentially flood-prone structures.

### Documented inundation risk at City-selected locations

The available information does not identify the selected mitigation concept for this application. [Information needed: Confirm the flood-risk mitigation concept that the City of Richfield is submitting for the Flood Hazard Mitigation Grant Assistance Program application.]

The planning report identifies the following flood-risk conditions at the three locations selected by the City for concept-level evaluation:

- **Near Wilson Pond:** The report identifies this as one of the locations with the largest flood risk in the city. It affects the most residential structures in a single location; the lowest structures are affected during the 2-year, 24-hour rainfall event; the area has a high social vulnerability index; and surface inundation affects a critical transportation route and a school.
- **Northwest of Roosevelt Park:** The report states that this flood-risk area affects multiple structures in one location. The lowest structures are affected during the 10-year, 24-hour rainfall event; the area has a high social vulnerability index; and surface inundation affects a critical transportation route.
- **Near Woodlawn Terrace:** The report states that this flood-risk area affects multiple structures in one location. The lowest structures are affected during the 2-year, 24-hour rainfall event; storm sewer pipes are classified as moderate to high risk; the area has a high social vulnerability index; and surface inundation affects three high-density housing structures.

### Evidence limitations and supporting documentation

The reported conditions are model-based estimates of potential inundation and potentially flood-prone structures. The report states that no survey data was collected to verify flood-prone structures; subsequent feasibility-stage surveys may show that existing structures are or are not flood-prone. The available information does not document observed flood damage, damage values, repair costs, or displacement for the three locations evaluated in the planning report.

The updated PCSWMM model incorporates 2022 USGS LiDAR data, information on construction projects with stormwater impacts since 2018, updated City GIS storm-sewer data and as-built drawings where available, updated storm lift-station data, and the Taft Park storm pump station.

The report evaluates six concept-level flood-risk reduction alternatives at three City-selected locations: near Wilson Pond, northwest of Roosevelt Park, and near Woodlawn Terrace. ## Project description

### Immediate-phase objective

The August 2025 *Stormwater Model Update and Flood-Risk Area Identification and Prioritization* report identifies six concept-level flood-risk mitigation alternatives at three City-selected locations: near Wilson Pond, northwest of Roosevelt Park, and near Woodlawn Terrace. The available information does not identify which alternative is proposed for this Flood Hazard Mitigation Grant Assistance Program application.

[Information needed: Confirm the flood-risk mitigation concept that the City of Richfield is submitting for the Flood Hazard Mitigation Grant Assistance Program application.]

[Information needed: Confirm the current-phase objective for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Basis for the proposed project

The City of Richfield reviewed the flood-risk prioritization and selected three locations for planning-level evaluation. For each location, concept-level projects were modeled to evaluate flood-risk reduction, and planning-level cost estimates were developed for City staff to consider in further evaluation.

The report describes the alternatives as concept-level designs. It states that each alternative provides some level of flood-risk mitigation, with varied costs and additional project considerations.

### Later-phase considerations

The planning report states that additional evaluations will be needed as a mitigation concept is pursued. These include design optimization, utility-conflict evaluation, permitting review, and, in some cases, agreements with private landowners or other public entities.

For any selected Wilson Pond alternative, the report states that increased flow to Highway 494 would need to be conveyed to the Minnesota River through the City of Bloomington or along the Highway 494 corridor. Routing beyond the Richfield municipal boundary has not been determined; further coordination with the City of Bloomington or MnDOT and additional permitting discussions would be required if the City advances a Wilson Pond concept.

The report identifies project-specific considerations for other alternatives. The Northwest of Roosevelt Park alternative would require storm-sewer modifications to direct drainage to an underground storage chamber. The Woodlawn Terrace underground-storage alternative would require parking-lot regrading and an agreement with the owner of the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments.

### Partners and roles

The City of Richfield selected the three locations for planning-level evaluation and provided the prioritization scoring and weighting criteria used in the report. Barr Engineering Co. prepared the August 2025 planning report for the City.

title: Project analysis
body_markdown:
## Project analysis

### Alternatives and feasibility

The August 2025 *Stormwater Model Update and Flood-Risk Area Identification and Prioritization* report presents concept-level alternatives at three City-selected flood-risk areas. The alternatives were modeled to assess flood-risk reduction, and planning-level cost estimates were developed for further City consideration. The report states that additional design and evaluation will be required before an alternative is pursued.

[Information needed: Confirm the flood-risk mitigation concept that the City of Richfield is submitting for the Flood Hazard Mitigation Grant Assistance Program application.]

At Wilson Pond, the report evaluated three alternatives: Concept A would lower the pond water level ahead of a storm event, lower the outlet invert, and increase downstream storm-sewer capacity; Concept B would increase storm-sewer capacity using a single 5-foot by 5-foot box culvert from Wilson Pond to Highway 494; and Concept C would use two parallel 5-foot by 5-foot box culverts along that route. The report considered but did not pursue surface storage because of limited undeveloped space and the City's direction not to consider property acquisition for flood-risk reduction. It did not pursue underground storage because shallow groundwater is expected in the area, and it did not pursue a pump because the assumed 24-hour drawdown period would require a high pumped flow rate for a stormwater system.

For Wilson Pond Concept A, modeled peak water levels were lower than existing conditions by 1.9, 0.1, and 4.2 feet at Wilson Pond, upstream at East 73rd Street and South 17th Avenue, and downstream at East 75th Street and South 15th Avenue, respectively, for the 2-year, 24-hour storm. For the 10-year, 24-hour storm, the corresponding modeled reductions were 1.4, 0.8, and 3.9 feet; for the 100-year, 24-hour storm, they were 0.3 feet at each of the three locations.

For Wilson Pond Concepts B and C, the model shows increased backflow in the pipe out of Wilson Pond during the 2-year, 24-hour event, resulting in higher modeled peak water levels in Wilson Pond. Both concepts reduce modeled peak water levels at the downstream location for the evaluated 2-, 10-, and 100-year, 24-hour events. All Wilson Pond concepts assume sufficient capacity to route additional flow away from Richfield. The report states that the routing to the Minnesota River through Bloomington or along the Highway 494 corridor has not been determined and would require coordination with the City of Bloomington or MnDOT and additional permitting discussions.

Northwest of Roosevelt Park, the report identifies one alternative: an underground storage chamber beneath the Roosevelt Park baseball fields. The concept would provide approximately 354,000 cubic feet of storage, based on a 300-foot by 300-foot area, a 5.25-foot depth, and an assumed 75% available storage volume. An outlet-control structure would retain runoff during a storm and allow the chamber to drain after the event. For the 2-, 10-, and 100-year, 24-hour storms, the modeled water-level reductions range from 0.4 to 4.6 feet across the three reported model locations. Surface storage and increased downstream capacity were considered but not pursued because the undeveloped portion of Roosevelt Park is at a higher elevation than the flood-risk area, gravity drainage to a potential pond was not feasible, and the area drains to Norby's Pond, which is also identified as a flood-risk area.

Near Woodlawn Terrace, the report evaluates an underground storage chamber beneath the parking lot next to Lynwood Commons Apartments and an alternative to increase storm-sewer capacity from the parking lot to Wood Lake. The storage alternative would provide approximately 24,000 cubic feet of storage, based on approximately 8,000 square feet of surface area, a 3-foot depth, and an assumed 75% available storage volume. It would require parking-lot regrading, storm-sewer modifications, and an agreement with the parking-lot owner. The storage concept reduces modeled peak water levels by 0.0 to 0.6 feet across the reported locations and storm events. The storm-sewer alternative would increase pipe diameters from a current range of 3 to 4 feet to a range of 3 to 6 feet; modeled reductions range from 0.0 to 1.1 feet across the reported locations and storm events. Surface storage was considered but not pursued because the open space is developed with baseball fields and parking lots.

The report characterizes each alternative as a concept-level design. As an alternative advances, it identifies needs for design optimization, utility-conflict evaluation, permitting review and, in some cases, agreements with private landowners or other public entities.

### Environmental effects

The available planning report does not provide an environmental-effects assessment for the specific alternative proposed in this application. It notes that permitting requirements require further review as a concept advances. For Wilson Pond alternatives, downstream routing beyond the Richfield municipal boundary has not been determined. The report also identifies expected shallow groundwater as a reason underground storage was not considered near Wilson Pond.

[Information needed: Provide the environmental effects assessment for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Social and economic effects

The planning report's prioritization framework includes the CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI). It describes social vulnerability as a measure of a community's ability to respond to a natural disaster and uses SVI data to identify areas that may need support before, during, and after hazardous events.

The three areas evaluated for concept-level alternatives are located in areas with a high SVI. The Wilson Pond area affects the most residential structures in a single location and surface inundation affects a critical transportation route and a school. The Northwest of Roosevelt Park area affects multiple structures and a critical transportation route. Near Woodlawn Terrace, surface inundation affects three high-density housing structures.

These findings are model-based prioritization information and do not quantify the selected project's beneficiaries, economic damages avoided, or effects on underserved communities.

[Information needed: Provide the social and economic effects assessment for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Public input

The available planning report states that City staff reviewed the prioritization results and identified three locations for planning-level evaluation. It does not document public engagement, public comments, or responses to public input for the selected project.

[Information needed: Provide the public-input record for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Environmental review

The planning report identifies permitting review as work to be completed as an alternative is pursued, but it does not state the environmental-review status for the selected project.

[Information needed: Confirm the environmental-review status for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Water-plan alignment

The prioritization framework is intended to help the City compare potential benefits of flood-risk mitigation projects and inform future flood-risk mitigation studies. It considers storm-system conditions, critical infrastructure, flooding frequency, social vulnerability, and potentially flood-prone structures. The report does not identify a local water-management plan or cite a plan provision applicable to the selected project.

[Information needed: Provide the local water-management plan reference that supports the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]

### Wetland-replacement-credit intent

The available planning report does not state whether the selected project would require wetland replacement credits or whether the City intends to purchase, use, or generate such credits.

[Information needed: Confirm the wetland-replacement-credit intent for the selected Richfield flood-risk mitigation project.]
